newsitem.title: INDIA: India PM says no plan for talks with separatists.
newsitem.headline: India PM says no plan for talks with separatists.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral, on his first visit to the troubled Kashmir region since assuming office, said on Sunday he had no plans to start talks with a leading organisation of separatists.
"The process of normalisation is under way. The elected government is firmly saddled," Gujral told reporters at Jammu, winter capital of the state of Jammu and Kashmir.
Last year, India held local elections after a gap of nine years in Kashmir in a bid to revive democracy. The regional National Conference party swept the election.

When asked if he intended to hold talks with a 30-party organisation of of Kashmiri separatists, the All-Parties' Hurriyat (freedom) Conference, ahead of a meeting with Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharief next month, he replied: "There are no plans."
Pakistan and India have fought two wars over Kashmir since both countries gained independence from Britain in 1947.

Islamabad denies Indian charges that it arms separatists who in 1990 launched a major offensive in the state, mainly Hindu India's only Moslem majority province. It says it provides only moral and diplomatic support to guerrillas.

"The process of dialogue between India and Pakistan was underway and the talks had been held at foreign secretaries and ministerial levels," Gujral said, referring to a resumption last month of talks stalled for three years.
Gujral and Sharif are expected to meet on the fringes of a summit of the seven-nation South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation in the Maldives in May.
Gujral's choice of the state for his first trip out of the capital as prime minister was seen as a signal that Kashmir was on his list of priorities.
During his visit to the predominantly Hindu Jammu region, he visited a camp of Hindu migrants who fled the Moslem-majority Kashmir valley during the rebellion. He appealed for religious harmony.
"The state of Jammu and Kashmir does not belong to any particular community," he said.
Gujral urged the people of Kashmir to shed sectarian feelings and concentrate on economic development.
He said India needed to boost economic growth and at the same time step up poverty alleviation programmes to achieve the objective of social justice for all.
Since 1990, when simmering discontent erupted into a major rebellion, more than 20,000 people have been killed in Kashmir.
India controls two thirds of the region while Pakistan controls the remaining third.

Gujral was sworn in as the country's 12th prime minister last Monday after his United Front changed its previous leader, H.D. Deve Gowda, in order to win back vital parliamentary support from the Congress party.
